findings.claim: A fresh browser mount registers the per-session handlers before sending subscribe. The server then registers the socket as a subscriber, obtains the snapshot, sends screen-snapshot, and only afterward sends subscribed with ready=false. The client applies/replaces the terminal and ACKs with replayToken before the server marks the session ready.

The authoritative server snapshot intentionally contains only the active viewport: xterm-headless may retain configured scrollback, but serialization defaults to {scrollback: 0}. In the checked config the headless retention is 1,000 logical lines, yet none of that retained history is transferred on refresh.

findings.claim: The browser fallback cache is also viewport-only. It saves SerializeAddon output with scrollback=0 as schemaVersion=2/payloadKind=viewport-only plus sessionId, content, cols, rows, bufferType, and savedAt. Restore requires exact cols/rows equality; authoritative replacement calls term.reset(), so a refreshed xterm starts with only the restored viewport even though its live in-memory scrollback cap is hard-coded to 10,000 lines.

The exact default/current limits form mismatched loss boundaries: server headless scrollback=1,000 (schema range 0..50,000), browser live scrollback=10,000, server snapshot=2,097,152 UTF-8 bytes (schema 1,024..268,435,456), local snapshot=2,000,000 characters, all local snapshots=3,000,000 characters/16 entries, and local parser newlines<=4*rows. PTY geometry defaults to 80x24 and is capped at 500x200.

findings.claim: When server viewport serialization exceeds maxSnapshotBytes, it rejects the whole payload rather than clipping it: data becomes empty and truncated=true. WsRouter labels this empty healthy snapshot as fallback. The client then tries the local viewport cache; if unavailable it resets to a BuilderGate placeholder. This directly explains a blank/stale/truncated screen after refresh, and multibyte output reaches the byte cap earlier than the browser character cap.

findings.claim: The local fallback can be stale or absent independently of the server: a newly serialized viewport over perSnapshotMaxChars is refused while the previous snapshot is retained; malformed, oversized, wrong-session, empty, wrong-geometry-shape, or >4*rows-newline payloads are rejected and cleared; projected storage over budget fails the save after eviction attempts.

The normal subscribe race is fenced correctly. ReplayPendingState is installed before screen-snapshot is sent; live output produced afterward is queued rather than sent; after matching ACK the queued output is emitted before session:ready. This prevents ordinary post-snapshot output from being erased by client term.reset().

findings.claim: That replay fence is lossy under sustained output: its queue limit is min(maxSnapshotBytes, 262,144 bytes), append keeps only a UTF-8-safe tail, and queuedOutputTruncated is observational only. After ACK or the fixed 5-second timeout, only the retained tail is flushed. Losing an ANSI prefix or earlier repaint can leave the reconstructed screen semantically wrong even if the latest plain text is present.

findings.claim: During the 300 ms React remount/unsubscribe grace window, WebSocketContext buffers output without a size cap, but receipt of any screen-snapshot replaces the buffered snapshot and unconditionally clears all earlier buffered output. This is safe only when the arriving snapshot covers that output; an empty/oversized fallback does not, so output can be dropped during a handler handoff even though full-refresh subscribe ordering is fenced.

Hidden terminals intentionally skip live writes under the default snapshot-restore policy. On visibility they first restore the stale local viewport and then request a viewport-only screen repair. Output produced while hidden therefore never enters the browser's 10,000-line scrollback, even when the current viewport is eventually repaired.

Visible browser output also has a bounded loss path: defaults are 4,194,304 queued bytes, 512 chunks, and 262,144 bytes per flush budget. Overflow drops the enqueue, marks the terminal stale, and requests screen repair; repair is viewport-only, so it restores current screen state but cannot restore lost scrollback.

findings.claim: Server-side headless lag has another bounded degradation path. Defaults permit 8,388,608 pending bytes or 1,024 chunks; overflow degrades the headless authority. Its cached viewport plus unsnapshotted and pending output are concatenated and tail-truncated to maxSnapshotBytes, then exposed as fallback raw data. This preserves bounded recent output, not a guaranteed terminal-state-equivalent snapshot.

minimal_reproduction.name: intentional refresh scrollback loss

Scroll upward and confirm the first marker exists in the live xterm scrollback.
Hard-refresh the browser and reopen the same session without resizing.
Observe that the current viewport is reconstructed but early markers are absent; neither the server snapshot nor local cache contains scrollback.

unknowns.item: The code alone cannot identify which boundary caused a reported instance. Correlate snapshot_serialized truncated/byteLength, replay queuedOutputTruncated, fallback mode, and frontend screen_snapshot_* debug events for the affected session.

It is unverified in a real browser whether snapshot application can exceed the 5-second server ACK timeout under a large ANSI payload, IME wait, or saturated main thread. The timeout releases queued output regardless of client apply completion.
Browser-specific localStorage quota and eviction behavior remains environment-dependent; the code retries quota failures and may retain the previous current-session snapshot.

The client resource schema exposes terminal.scrollbackLines, but TerminalView instantiation is hard-coded to 10,000 and Settings capability tests mark that setting unavailable; whether dynamic configurability is intended is not established by the focused files.
